newsitem.title: POLAND: Martial law row swirls around Polish army chief.
newsitem.headline: Martial law row swirls around Polish army chief.

text.p: Solidarity veterans denounced the choice this week of General Henryk Szumski to lead Poland's armed forces into NATO, recalling his role in enforcing the 1981 communist martial law decree which crushed the union.
President Aleksander Kwasniewski on Monday sacked chief of general staff Tadeusz Wilecki and appointed Szumski, who was billed as better suited to adapt the army to NATO requirements.

This astounded former interior minister Andrzej Milczanowski, who spent more than two years in a communist jail after tanks under the then colonel Szumski smashed the gates of the Szczecin shipyard where he was a Solidarity strike leader.
"So the Polish army is supposed to be brought into NATO by a man who at the start of martial law pacified the striking Szczecin shipyard in which there were 9,000 workers," he said.

"This is a consummate scandal, an insult to common sense, I'll say more -- it is cheek," said Milczanowski who quit the cabinet in December 1995 after the election defeat of the previous president, former Solidarity chief Lech Walesa.
Defence Ministry spokesman Eugeniusz Mleczak said on Thursday that Szumski had followed orders, like other soldiers, when General Wojciech Jaruzelski clamped martial law on Poland in December 1981.
He said that far from pacifying the yard, a term which in Polish implies repression, Szumski had eased confrontation.
"He fulfilled the tasks demanded by martial law like all other soldiers at the time, who had no choice," he added.
But the Solidarity union branch in Szczecin said in a statement quoted by Thursday's Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper that Szumski had been enthusiastic in denouncing the union.
"For Szczecin people General Szumski is associated with the use of the army to defend Communist Party interests," it said.
Jaruzelski, now ill in hospital, has long argued that he had to clamp down on Solidarity, the Soviet bloc's first free trade union, to avoid a hugely bloody Soviet invasion.
While this view is often disputed, opinion polls show that a majority of Poles now believe martial law was justified.
A diplomat from a NATO member state, who asked not to be named, said the Western pact was unlikely to be concerned over the martial law chapter of 56-year-old Szumski's past.
Years after the 1989 fall of communism, most senior Polish officers, including him and Wilecki, are still Moscow-trained.
Kwasniewski fired Wilecki after a peak in the general's rows with the government which is led by ex-communists.

These partly concerned Wilecki's efforts to circumvent reforms introduced last year to improve the civilian defence ministry's control of the military -- one condition the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation looks for in new members.
